resources.string: Booting a real OS means running a second kernel under emulation — its own kernel, its own init, its own userland and uid space. That is genuinely a ROM booting, just slowly. There are three ways to do it, two gated by a privilege a sideloaded app cannot hold; the chain below probes all three and names what it finds.
This is not the Linux subsystem

The per-app Termux prefix runs a Linux userland at full native speed because it shares Android\'s kernel — the right answer for packages, daemons and toolchains. A ROM is the wrong tool for those and the only tool for running an OS whose kernel differs from Android\'s. If you want a package, you want the subsystem, not this.
AVF → KVM → QEMU TCG → ABSENT. Probed in order; the best available is the one in use, and each closed path names what it lacks.
No ROM backend available in this build
Every path is closed on a stock sideloaded build, so there is nothing to launch. Each reason below names exactly what is missing:
Images live in app-scoped external storage, not the prefix — they are measured in gigabytes and survive a prefix rebuild. None are bundled; add your own.
No ROM images added. Pick an OS image (postmarketOS, Alpine, Android-x86 …) and it is copied here.
Copying the image into app storage… this is a real file copy and can take a while for a multi-gigabyte image.
Launch is disabled because no ROM backend is available in this build — see the reasons above. A disabled control that names what is missing is the honest state here; there is no faked boot.
